blogs.title: Multiphasic Mayhem: Managing Anaphylaxis That Keeps Coming Back
blogs.description: Using a clarithromycin-triggered case with four relapses, this post walks through distinguishing biphasic, multiphasic, and refractory anaphylaxis, and weighs repeated IM epinephrine versus an IV epinephrine infusion. We’ll outline bedside decision points, monitoring needs, and how to pivot as episode intensity evolves.

blogs.title: The Adult Dose We Keep Missing: Why 0.5 mg IM Epinephrine Matters
blogs.description: Many adults are underdosed with 0.3 mg auto-injectors despite guideline-recommended 0.5 mg. We review the weight-based rationale, emerging outcome data favoring 0.5 mg, and practical fixes: stocking 0.5 mg options, prefilled syringes, dosing prompts in order sets, and training to overcome hesitancy.

blogs.title: Steroids in Anaphylaxis: Habit, Hype, or Harm?
blogs.description: This case received steroids after recurrence, reflecting common practice—yet evidence increasingly shows no prevention of biphasic reactions and possible harms. We synthesize the literature, clarify when (if ever) steroids have a role, and emphasize epinephrine-first management and appropriate observation instead.

blogs.title: How Long Is Long Enough? Risk-Stratified Observation After Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Observation recommendations remain inconsistent, but half of biphasic events occur within 6–12 hours. We translate guideline differences into a pragmatic, tiered ED/ICU pathway using clinical predictors (severity, hypotension, multiple epinephrine doses) to decide 4–6, 12, or 24+ hour monitoring and when ICU makes sense.

blogs.title: Tryptase Timing Pearls: Don’t Miss the 20% + 2
blogs.description: Suboptimal sampling in this case limited interpretation. We cover when and how to collect acute and baseline tryptase, apply the 20% + 2 rule, and use results to confirm mast cell activation, guide documentation, and trigger downstream evaluation for mast cell disorders.

blogs.title: Unmasking Mast Cell Disease After Severe Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Persistent baseline tryptase elevation and severe, recurrent anaphylaxis should prompt a workup for clonal mast cell disorders. We review when to suspect systemic mastocytosis, what initial tests and referrals to consider, counseling on triggers, and why patients can be high risk even without meeting full diagnostic criteria.

blogs.title: Auto-Injectors Inside the Hospital: Speed vs Dose Accuracy
blogs.description: Auto-injectors reduce delay and cognitive load but often deliver 0.3 mg in adults who need 0.5 mg. We discuss when auto-injectors are helpful as a bridge, needle-length considerations, and how to build protocols that rapidly transition to correctly dosed IM epinephrine or IV infusion in monitored settings.

blogs.title: Biphasic, Refractory, or Ongoing Absorption? Getting the Labels Right
blogs.description: Not every relapse is biphasic: persistent exposure or slow absorption from long-acting or oral agents can mimic recurrence. We highlight bedside clues, timelines, and therapeutic implications—when to anticipate protracted courses, when to consider decontamination strategies, and how labels drive monitoring decisions.

blogs.title: When “Antibiotic Allergy” Steers You Wrong: Avoiding Anchoring After Drug Rashes
blogs.description: A late rash to clindamycin led to a clarithromycin switch and first-time anaphylaxis. We unpack pitfalls in attributing rashes to true allergy, lack of cross-reactivity assumptions, and safer pathways: deferring nonurgent antibiotics, allergy consultation, and precise documentation to improve future prescribing.
